title: Judge ready to reverse order removing Penman from council; won’t say if he should be reinstated
summary: Former Harford County Council member Aaron Penman inched closer Friday to potentially being returned to his former seat during a hearing in circuit court.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters May 29, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters May 29, 2026

Former Harford County Council member Aaron Penman inched closer Friday to being returned to his former seat after a hearing in circuit court.

Circuit Judge W. Michel Pierson vacated a 2025 order forcing Penman from office. But he stopped short of restoring the Republican to his former office.

“Mr. Penman seeks an order from the court placing him in a seat on the Harford County Council. That seat is not vacant,” Pierson said during a morning hearing. “It means that in order for the court to grant the order he seeks, the court would necessarily have to order the current occupant be removed from that seat.”

Penman was removed by a Harford County Circuit judge who ruled he could not serve on the council while also being employed as a deputy in the Harford County Sheriff’s Department. Alison Imhoff, a 39-year old social worker, was appointed by the Republican Central Committee to fill the vacancy.

“In my view, that person (Imhoff) is entitled to be heard on this issue,” Pierson said.

Penman, outside the courtroom, said he was pleased with Pierson’s order vacating the 2025 decision.

Penman wins appeal, reinstatement to seat on Harford County Council

The council is scheduled to meet next week. Penman said he had hoped to be reinstated by then. The clock is ticking on what remains of the term he was elected to in 2022.

The council will take a brief hiatus over the summer before returning to work in September. The council is up for election in November. The new term starts in December.

“It’s been two years now fighting for a seat that I was wrongfully removed from to begin with, and the courts have ruled that through the appeals court,” Penman said. “I just thought there would be a quicker process once the appeals court opinion was rendered for me to return to my seat. But we’re going through the legal process. It looks like there’s light at the end of the tunnel. I just hope we get there quickly.”

Penman was removed nearly 18 months ago after County Executive Bob Cassilly (R) challenged the deputy’s eligibility to serve.

The case was seen as an extension of an intraparty spat between Cassilly and Harford County Sheriff Jeff Gahler and an ongoing and related dispute between the executive and the Republican-controlled council.

Penman was the second county legislator Cassilly attempted to block from serving.

In 2022, Cassilly tried to keep Jacob Bennett (D) from being sworn in. Cassilly said Bennet’s job as a middle school science teacher in Harford County violated prohibitions on being on the council while working in a government position.

Harford County Circuit Court Judge Richard S. Bernhardt Sr. sided with Cassilly and said Bennet had to choose. Bennett opted to not resign from his teaching job. Instead, he appealed the ruling.

The Supreme Court of Maryland disagreed in April 2023, clearing the way for Bennett to be sworn in.

Ironically, it was Bernhardt who ruled that Penman was ineligible to serve.

The Appellate Court of Maryland ruled in April that Bernhardt wrongfully removed Penman. Much of that opinion cited the earlier ruling involving Bennett.

After a brief recess, Pierson returned to court with his two orders.

Harford County Attorney Jeff Blomquist unsuccessfully argued to Pierson that vacating the order removing Penman was premature. The county has appealed the ruling to the Maryland Supreme Court.

“We don’t even have a final order,” Blomquist told Pierson. “We’re talking about an Appellate Court order that is not final.”

Pierson rejected the argument.

“I disagree with you,” Pierson told Blomquist. “I rely on 25 years of knowledge that the decision of the Appellate Court is final. The decision by the Supreme Court to review it is discretionary.”

Imhoff, who works in Towson, traveled to Bel Air during the recess. She appeared in court where Pierson served her with his order, adding her to the case. She has 15 days to respond.

“I do believe in due process, and I do trust that the judge will explore every detail of this case and be able to make it into a law for us to be able to move forward with,” Imhoff said outside the courtroom.

Pierson did not ask Imhoff during the hearing if she would contest her own removal. The central committee made it clear when they filled the vacancy that her service could be temporary. If Penman was successful in his appeal, he might go back to the council, she said.

Penman filed to run for his former seat in the 2026 election. He later withdrew his candidacy when the appeals court had not issued a ruling as the deadline to withdraw approached.

Penman has since endorsed Imhoff, who is running to keep the seat to which she was appointed.

It seems unlikely she will contest an order that restores Penman to his seat.

“I understand what my community and ethical obligations are, not just with this case, but with my role as a council member, and I do trust due process,” Imhoff said. “It has been my honor to be able to serve District B, and I hope to do that for the future. But Aaron Penman was elected to the seat. I respect that. I respect the voice of the voters. So, we’re, we’re trying to figure out the cleanest and best path forward.”
